Inordinate

in-OR-dih-nit -- from Latin inordinatus, in- ('not') + ordinatus ('arranged, set in order'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inordinate is unusually large or excessive, well beyond what is normal or reasonable.

The new employee handbook devoted an inordinate number of pages to the office's parking policy, far more than to actual job duties.

Worked Example

For a dish that took ten minutes to cook, the recipe demanded an inordinate number of specialty ingredients that most home cooks would never have on hand.

That sense of something being far more than the situation reasonably calls for -- too much time, too many steps, too high a price -- is exactly what inordinate describes.

How Inordinate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

excessive

excessive: more than is necessary or reasonable

disproportionate

disproportionate: too large or small in relation to something else

Antonyms

reasonable

reasonable: fair and sensible, within normal limits

modest

modest: not excessive or exaggerated in amount

How Strong Is It? — excessive → inordinate → disproportionate

excessive vs. inordinate

excessive vs. inordinate: The fine seemed excessive for what was, after all, a first offense.

disproportionate vs. inordinate

disproportionate vs. inordinate: Critics called the punishment disproportionate to the minor rule the student had broken.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of inordinate.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — ordin-

root — ordin-: order, rank, arrangement (Latin (ordo))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: having, marked by; forms an adjective (Latin (-atus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin in- ('not') plus ordo ('order, rank') plus the adjective suffix -ate: 'not kept in order.' Something inordinate has spilled past its proper bounds -- far beyond what is fitting.

Use the root in a new word: ordinary

Use the root in a new word: ordinary: There was nothing ordinary about the storm -- it dropped more rain in an hour than the town usually saw in a month.

Root Check

Word Choice

Inordinate always signals a judgment that something has gone beyond a reasonable limit -- an inordinate amount of time, attention, or cost -- it's rarely used for something that's simply large in a neutral, unremarkable way.
